Opinion Academia Poland and ASEAN deepen a growing partnership Poland's accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (TAC) is a clear statement that peace, dialogue and respect for international law remain the best foundations for security in an increasingly uncertain world. Share this article Change text size Gift Premium Articles to Anyone P oland's accession to the Treaty of Amity and Cooperation (TAC), formalized on July 24 at the 59th ASEAN Foreign Ministers' Meeting in Manila, marks more than a diplomatic milestone. It is a clear statement that peace, dialogue and respect for international law remain the best foundations for security in an increasingly uncertain world. By joining the TAC, Poland joins the growing community of countries and organizations that recognize ASEAN's principles as the foundation for engaging with Southeast Asia. Poland joined the Treaty alongside three close European partners, namely, Sweden, Romania and Lithuania. Like Poland, these countries understand that security in today's interconnected world cannot be built only within our own neighborhood. It also requires closer dialogue with trusted partners such as ASEAN, whose central role in maintaining peace and stability in Southeast Asia has never been more important. Our engagement with ASEAN has been steadily growing. Poland maintains one of the largest diplomatic networks in the Indo-Pacific among Central European countries, with 14 embassies, six consulates general and 12 trade and investment offices. By 2025, trade between Poland and ASEAN exceeded US$13 billion annually, around 30,000 citizens of ASEAN countries - primarily from Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia - were legally employed in Poland, and more than 1,000 students from ASEAN pursued higher education at Polish universities every year. Poland sees ASEAN not only as one of the world's fastest-growing economic regions, but also as an indispensable partner in addressing common challenges, from connectivity and digital transformation to energy transition and regional security. Having successfully transformed its economy over the past three decades, becoming the world's 20th largest economy, Poland is ready to share its experience in modernization, digital public services and sustainable growth. The lessons of recent years, from the pandemic and supply-chain disruptions to Russia's war against Ukraine, have made one thing clear: resilience, whether economic or security-related, is built through international cooperation and begins far beyond Europe's borders. In recent years, Poland has emerged as one of Europe's most committed and credible security partners. This is reflected not only in words, but also in action: Poland is among NATO allies with the highest levels of defense spending as a share of gross domestic product, plays a key role in strengthening the Alliance's eastern flank and has provided substantial political, military and humanitarian support to Ukraine following Russia's full-scale invasion. These experiences have reinforced Poland's belief that security requires solidarity, preparedness and cooperation among reliable partners – principles that also lie at the heart of ASEAN's approach to regional stability. https://www.prnewswire.com/news-releases.text: Fundway (fundwayplatform.com) is live, being the first platform where fund managers see fund costs across global jurisdictions and connect with leading service providers. BRATISLAVA, Slovakia , Aug. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fundway ( fundwayplatform.com ) went live today as the first platform where fund managers can see what it costs to set up and run a fund across global jurisdictions and connect directly with leading service providers to make it happen. For years, the fund industry remained and operated as closed circuit, unavailable to approach by emerging fund managers, looking to launch a fund. Everyone who tried to, also knows the problem - the prices remain hidden and unknown for a while. A manager planning their first fund has to request quotes one by one, from administrators, lawyers and auditors, and the answers arrive slowly, in different formats, with wide ranges, variables and plenty of "it depends." It can take weeks to arrive at a number solid enough for a business plan, and even then the search for the right firms is still ahead. Fundway completely flips the script and changed this industry wide problem. Simply answer a few questions about the fund you have in mind: strategy, size, expected numbers of investors and transactions, valuation frequency, launch timeline and distribution regions. Within seconds, you receive a cost breakdown, and alongside it, quotes from verified providers matched to your fund who are ready to take it from plan to launch. "We kept hearing the same story from people trying to start their first fund. They spent more time finding out what things cost, and who to even call, than deciding whether the fund made sense," said Cyril Oresansky, Fundway's founder. "Fundway answers both questions at once. Here is what it costs, and here are the firms who can do it." Bolder Group and Funds Avenue / Trustmoore have already joined as major verified partners, with more industry leaders already being in advanced discussions. Verified partners give Fundway their actual fee schedules, so the numbers on the platform come from the providers themselves. When a manager is ready, they connect with their chosen provider in one click, and the provider responds with a tailored proposal. "Emerging managers bring a great deal of energy and fresh thinking to the funds industry, but they often need practical support early on, before the fund is even launched. As a boutique administrator, we have always tried to be close to that part of the market, to offer accessible guidance and flexibility to newer managers. Such partnership with Fundway is another way for us to stay connected to managers at the point where good advice can make a real difference," said Jeroen van Zanten, Global Head of Growth, Bolder Group. Fundway is free for both seasoned and emerging fund managers and earns its revenue from provider partnerships. It covers hedge funds, private equity, venture capital, real estate, private credit, digital assets and family office structures, across the Cayman Islands, Delaware, Luxembourg, Ireland, Singapore, the UK, Switzerland and dozens of other domiciles. Fundway is the first platform to compare fund setup and management costs across global jurisdictions and connect managers with verified service providers. It was founded by Cyril Oresansky and is based in Bratislava. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c670.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Helen Haines had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack By Chris Graham Published 8 hours ago The condition of Helen Haines, the Australian MP hit by a car five days ago in north-east Victoria, has improved from critical to serious but stable. The independent MP, 65, had both her legs amputated after what authorities say was a deliberate attack outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, north-east of Melbourne, on Monday. In the latest update on Saturday morning, the Alfred Hospital in Melbourne said Haines was in a serious but stable condition, the first improvement since she was airlifted there. Her alleged attacker, 43-year-old Brendan Nugent, was arrested shortly after the incident and has since appeared in court on three charges. The politician's husband, Phil Haines, said on Wednesday that the "horrendous incident" had caused his wife significant injuries but "her heart and her mind" were "in good shape". Figure caption, Shock and disbelief: How the attack on an Australian MP unfolded in a small rural town Nugent, who was arrested moments after he allegedly drove his Toyota LandCruiser into the MP, appeared in court to face three charges: dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury, and causing harm to a Commonwealth public official. Police said more charges might be laid, including attempted murder. His lawyer said his client had "mental health concerns" but did not give any further detail. Victoria Police has said its investigation, with support from the Australian Federal Police, remains ongoing and a motive is yet to be established. Investigators are looking into whether drug use or medication played a part in the incident. Nugent's family has said they were long-time friends with Haines. Shortly after the alleged attack, Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told ABC television that there had been a "rise in temperature" and "too much shouting, not enough discourse" in Australia. Haines, known for stances such as supporting stronger climate action, entered parliament in 2019 after working as a nurse and midwife. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Police officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026. Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Protest Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? Catherine De Vries Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better Mon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 04.29 EDT Share E urope is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris to Milan to Madrid share is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools. The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap election called after parliament voted down key housing reforms . France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher. At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leaves Europe with a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad? If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table. But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible. The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick. The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone – as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty – changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit. 1:44 Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – video But the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted. Negotiations over the next seven-year budget, worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist. Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching, Emmanuel Macron has urged fellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him. Le Pen no longer talks about taking France out of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget. Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | Editorial Read more Younger Europeans, in particular, face growing uncertainty about their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU. Recent polling suggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act. This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by. Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid.
